title: Shaar HaYichud 1: contemplation, and the depth, length and width of an idea
overview: Chapter 1 opens with *hisbonenus*, the contemplation that studies an idea until it is clear in its depth, using *iyun* as its tool. Every idea has depth, length and width. *Bina* explains an idea: it gives length by bringing it down to examples a child can grasp, and width by explaining it from every side. Its depth reaches up to the spring of *chachma*, the flash of a new idea. The levels then run from *chachma*, beyond any one idea, through *havein behachma*, the power to understand one thing from another, and *bina sheb'bina* and *chachma sheb'bina*, to the crown of *bina*, the depth of the concept. *Daas* is the personal bond with an idea. It carries a person through the details, with its own length, width and depth. That depth is reached through the focus of *amkus hadaas*, which narrows where *bina* spreads; each needs the other. Moshe, who was a person of *daas*, merited *bina* and the *shaar hanun*. The last class turns to *ahavas Yisrael*, the essence of the Baal Shem Tov's approach, and to the Alter Rebbe's answer to students of the Maggid who saw a departure in the Chabad approach.

terms.gloss: contemplation: studying an idea, dwelling on it, until it is understood clearly in its depth
close, in-depth study; the inner aspect of bina, which the Gemara calls iyun
the depth of daas: an intense focus that narrows onto one idea, the opposite of the spread of bina; the vessel for the depth of the idea
understanding: the grasp of an idea, developed through iyun into its length, width and depth
the flash of a new idea, the abstract essence before it becomes a system
the mind's personal bond with what it understands: the feeling that makes an idea one's own
the depth of the concept, which is the crown (keser) of bina
length: bringing an idea down to examples until a little child can grasp it
width: explaining an idea in many ways, from every side
understanding one idea from another, which comes from the depth of chachma
bina within bina: the iyun that clears every part of an idea, inner and outer
chachma within bina: inventing new perspectives within one grasp, which is the width

sections.title: Hisbonenus: contemplation is study until the idea is clear
sections.summary: *Hisbonenus* is the strong study of an idea, dwelling on it until it is understood in depth. It belongs to whatever level of the soul a person is on.

blocks.text: *Shaar HaYichud* is called the key to Chassidus. To begin understanding a topic you need its terminology, and in Chassidus that terminology comes from Kabbalah and the chain of descending worlds. To make it meaningful, a person must be able to turn the *mashal* into the *nimshal*, the point it stands for. That is why he calls the book the key.

blocks.title: The princess in the palace
blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: The Torah is like a princess sealed up in a palace: you have to find the way in, then the keys, and then unlock all the doors. He gives this *mashal* from *Me'am Lo'ez* and says that is the idea.

blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: The Mitteler Rebbe wrote books on *avoda* and on *haskala*, and for each he wrote a short introductory book. *Shaar HaYichud* introduces *haskala*; *Kuntres HaHispaalus* introduces *avoda*. Each branch has a beginner, an intermediate and an advanced book. Only two of his books are for all Chassidim: *Shaar HaYichud*, the key, and *Shaarei Orah*, the alef-beis of Chassidus. *Shaarei Orah* is a third branch, *havana*, understanding the reasons for the *mitzvos*.

blocks.question: In simple terms, what do *haskala* and *avoda* denote?
blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: *Haskala* is understanding G-d, or more broadly, understanding objective truths about reality. *Avoda* is understanding oneself, and gaining clarity and self-refinement through that understanding.

blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: The two are deeply intertwined and must go together: everything in *haskala* has to be brought to *avoda*. Still, the focus differs. *Haskala* is clarity about what is outside a person, seeing the world; *avoda* is mastering and refining oneself. In short, *haskala* works on the mind and *avoda* on the heart.

blocks.question: Is that difference like theory versus hands-on experience?
blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: There is some relation, but it is more than that. *Haskala* can and should be applied, and the difference is between the path of a *tzaddik* and the path of a *baal teshuva*. *Teshuva* here does not necessarily mean repentance for a sin.

blocks.title: Raw and cooked food
blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: The *Frierdiker Rebbe* gives a *mashal*. Some foods, fruit and vegetables, can be eaten raw and need only a little cooking to improve them. Meat and fish are dangerous raw and must be cooked thoroughly to become edible. In the same way, a *tzaddik* works mostly with what is already good and G-dly, and needs only a little enhancing, while a *baal teshuva* must work on what is bad in himself and in the world until it is useful.

blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: A *tzaddik*'s path lends itself more easily to spirituality: it is more secluded, a safer space to be connected. The *baal teshuva* takes a person's animal nature and the things of the world and refines them to be G-dly, which takes more effort and means dealing with evil and darkness. But there is a lot of overlap: each has *avoda*, and each has *haskala*.

blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: The books after *Kuntres HaHispaalus* in the *avoda* series are the three *Shaarei Teshuva*: volumes one and two, and *Derech Chaim*, which is volume three. The *haskala* series goes after *Shaar HaYichud* or *Shaar HaEmuna*, then *Atzeres Rosh* and *Imrei Binah*.

blocks.question: Is the reason to study *haskala* before *avoda* that the *avoda* books use terms only defined here?
blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: Not necessarily. This book is a sequel to *Kuntres HaHispaalus*, which introduces *avoda*. That tract says that to do *avoda* properly you need *hisbonenus*, so he wrote a book about *hisbonenus*. That tract's central theme is that we need a system to succeed at living these ideas, and this book explains the system.

blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: In *Tanya* the author first wrote the *haskala* section, *Shaar HaYichud VeHaEmuna*, and only then wrote *Likkutei Amarim*, but printed *Likkutei Amarim* first, since it is about *avoda*. So there is an idea of starting with *avoda*, with everything grounded in it and aimed at it.

blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: The Rebbe gave different paths depending on where a person comes from. Someone with a strong Torah background but not in Kabbalah and Chassidus gets one path; a young student in a Chabad yeshiva gets a slightly different one; a beginner in both gets another. The best order is the most natural one. Sometimes the Rebbe would have people learn *Tanya* in this order: *Shaarei Teshuva* of *Tanya* first, then *Shaar HaYichud VeHaEmuna*, then *Likkutei Amarim*.

blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: The logic of that order: the *Shaar HaTeshuva* of *Tanya* speaks of *avoda* in a way very relevant to most people. The advice in *Likkutei Amarim*, and in many places in Chassidus, needs a basic framework of understanding first.

blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: When *Kuntres HaHispaalus* and *Shaar HaYichud* were written, readers were at a high level of scholarship. They knew a lot of the *Zohar*, some of the Arizal's writings and other kabbalistic works, and *Reshis Chochma*, which was commonly learned then. So they were familiar with these concepts. Someone coming cold, with little knowledge, is in a different position from someone with a lot of knowledge who wants depth and to be able to use it.

blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: In the times of the Mitteler and Alter Rebbe there were great scholars. They learned a lot of Talmud and *Shulchan Aruch*, the kabbalistic books and the moral books, and they wanted depth and moral work. They wanted to daven with the deeper *kavanos* of the Arizal and to learn the reasons for the mitzvos from *Pri Eitz Chaim*. Were they really understanding it fully, how it fits together, and how to apply it?

blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: Chassidus was helping to open that up, though that was not its only purpose. The people learning it at that level had that scholarship. Nowadays many people learn Chassidus without the other source material it quotes, so it is a little different.

blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: Learning in order matters, and this book goes step by step from A to Z. But wherever you jump in, you have to learn enough to gather a critical mass of pieces before they start to connect. That means quantity, and also quality: go over the material several times, think about how the pieces fit, summarize and synthesize it. Mastery comes from that work.

blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: Books like this help, and so does a talk of the Rebbe that quotes these ideas: learned with the background, the talk is clarified and brought down to an accessible level. Learned without it, you miss the depth and nuance behind every word, since it builds on all those other sources. There is always more to learn, in quantity and in quality.

blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: This book follows *Kuntres HaHispaalus*, the introduction to the Chabad approach to *avoda*, especially in *davenen*, meditative prayer. It explains why a person needs a personal understanding of these ideas to change how he feels, refine his animal soul and unlock his G-dly soul.

blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: The Alter Rebbe's approach is the big thing in Chabad. In his view, the Baal Shem Tov and the Maggid wanted every person to go, as far as he can, through these ideas himself, so that he develops a real connection to G-dliness. That takes real learning, so the Mitteler Rebbe wrote *Shaar HaYichud* as an introduction to it.

blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: In that period the average person's background was much higher: they learned the *Zohar* and the Arizal, perhaps *Reshis Chochma*, and some of the writings of the *Ramak*. Still, they had trouble understanding and applying it. So Chassidus came to help people unlock it and show how they can understand and apply it.

blocks.outOfPlace: The class introduces the sefer before he reads chapter 1; placed under the first passage, which it leads into.
blocks.text: A book like this opens everything up, but it can be hard, since it quotes little bits and explains them a little. Without the background it takes work to become familiar with the concepts and see them used in different ways, until they feel natural. That takes breadth of learning, then the quality of reviewing and applying it until mastery. The first chapter or two teach how to learn this and how to learn anything. So, let's begin.

Line 1 says this is already explained at length in a special tract, *Kuntres HaHispaalus*: the excitement that contemplation, the thought born from it, brings to the mind and the heart. It works on the five levels of the soul, which he names in order.

The tract explains that, depending on a person's understanding and refinement, the effect goes either to the animal soul or to the G-dly soul. Within each there are the five levels, so the levels form a ladder that a person climbs as he develops a deeper and truer understanding.

The highest level runs through all of them: the *yechida*, the inner G-dly soul, gives a natural excitement and love for G-dliness at every level. What matters is to turn that on, to be true to yourself where you are, and to do what is natural at that level. It is not about reaching a certain level; wherever you are, it is supposed to be connected to *hisbonenus*.

phrases.en: So now, we need to explain what *hisbonenus* is

phrases.en: and how it should be done

phrases.en: So the essence, the definition of *hisbonenus*,

phrases.he: בעצם הוא ענין ההסתכלות החזקה בעמקות הענין ולעמוד עליו הרבה עד שיבין אותו על בוריו

blocks.text: Now the essence of *hisbonenus* is defined. In simple terms, it is to study an idea, to think about it and dwell on it until you understand it clearly, going through the process of learning something in depth.

He gives the terms: a strong look, the way one gazes or stares intently at the depth of an idea. That is not hearing, which belongs to *bina*, but a looking that comes from the level of *chachma*: the mind's eye sees the idea and experiences it, not only hears the words and masters them. That takes finding it in yourself, and dwelling on it until it is clear in all its parts, in minute detail.

sections.title: Iyun against girsa: depth needs dwelling, not a passing look
sections.summary: *Iyun* is the inner, in-depth study of *bina*, and *girsa* is the cursory first-impression reading. A passing glance at a building or an idea leaves almost nothing behind.

phrases.he: והוא בחינת פנימיות בינה
phrases.en: And so this is the inner process of *bina*

phrases.he: הנקרא בלשון הגמרא בשם עיון,
phrases.en: in *Gemara* terminology, we call this *iyun*, in-depth learning

phrases.he: כמו שאמר במסכת סוכה
phrases.en: like it says in *Sukka*

phrases.he: הא למגרס והא לעיוני
phrases.en: There's two types of study: there's a cursory study, which is just to amass knowledge, and then there's to really master the subject

phrases.he: פירוש הגירסא
phrases.en: The meaning of *girsa*, of cursory study, is

phrases.he: הוא רק הבנת הדבר בהשקפה ראשונה,
phrases.en: just to you learn it and you just understand it however your initial understanding is

phrases.he: שהולכת ונובעת במהירות בלתי עכוב והעמדה כלל
phrases.en: and you're just trying to cover ground quickly without stopping to dwell and think about any of the points for a long time

phrases.he: כידוע

blocks.text: *Bina* has an outer and an inner aspect. Learning something in a cursory way is the outer aspect of *bina*. Wanting to understand a thing to its depth, to master it and get its essence, is the inner aspect, and in the Gemara's terms that is *iyun*, in-depth learning.

To give a halachic ruling, to be able to *paskin*, it is not enough to know the basics. You need the inner reason: when a rule applies and when it does not. Often something looks like a textbook case where the halacha is plainly one way, and it turns out the other way, because once you understand the reason you see when it applies.
The Gemara in *Sukka* says: *hei l'migras, hei l'iyuni*. There are two kinds of study: a cursory one that only amasses knowledge, and one that really masters the subject.
The Rebbe advised that everyone should be fit to give a halachic ruling, at the level of knowledge and mastery that takes, and he laid out what to learn to get there.

The plan: first a general knowledge of the whole Torah, going through the whole *Mishneh Torah* of the *Rambam* and the whole *Mishnayos*, so you know all the topics. Then a set of tractates of Gemara, and a set of topics in halacha, learned in depth, so that you understand how to get to the depth of an idea and what it means to understand something. Then, when a new topic comes up, you know how to look it up and research it.

*Girsa* is cursory study: understanding something on first impression, learning it and grasping it however the first understanding goes, covering ground quickly without stopping to dwell on the points. You understand the basic *peshat* and go on.

phrases.he: על דרך משל המביט בעינו על דבר מה ואינו מתבונן כלל על הדבר
phrases.en: like if you just see something, you look something over quickly, but you don't think about it, you don't study it at all

phrases.he: באיכותו ומהותו בכל חלקיו הפנימים וחיצונים,
phrases.en: to really think about, you know, what it is, how it works, what makes it the way it is, all its details, its inside, its outside

phrases.he: רק דרך מעביר בעלמא
שבמשך זמן ודאי ישכח עליו לגמרי
phrases.en: So if a person just sees something and doesn't really think about it in depth, first of all, they're going to forget about it quickly

phrases.he: וגם לא יוכל לספר לזולתו
phrases.en: and also, if you want somebody else going to ask you what you saw, they can just say the general details, but they won't really be able to explain to somebody else because they just had a quick glance at it

phrases.he: רק כלליות ענין אותו הדבר שראה בהעברת העין
phrases.en: That's the idea that something he saw only with *haavaras ayin*, just a passing glance

phrases.he: ולא בטביעת עין כלל
phrases.en: *tviyas ayin* means, like when an expert looks at something and every detail they see has meaning

blocks.text: The *mashal* is someone who looks at something with his eye and does not think about it at all: he looks it over quickly and does not study it. To really know a thing you have to think about what it is, how it works, what makes it the way it is, all its details, inside and out.

blocks.title: The building you walk past
blocks.text: Reb Hillel Paritcher gives the example of someone who walks past a building and says, that's beautiful. To appreciate it, you would need an architect or someone with expertise to explain the proportions and what makes it have those qualities. In any field there is a big difference between someone with experience who knows what makes a thing work and someone who only sees it. Stories are the same: everybody knows a good one when they see it, but the craftsman knows how to make one.

blocks.question: If the point is to appreciate G-dliness, why can't I just take a walk outside, or believe and read books? Why do I have to really study and think?
blocks.text: In any subject, if you don't spend the time to analyze it, study it, compare and contrast, and plumb its depths, you won't get the mastery, the appreciation and the understanding that you get when you do.

Something seen only in passing is forgotten quickly. Learn a discourse, read it over once, say it over the Shabbos table, and it is gone. And you cannot explain it to someone else beyond the general details, because you had only a quick glance at it.

blocks.question: What is the connection between a superficial look and not remembering it for long?
blocks.text: Memory comes from *daas*, which is the feeling of a personal connection to an idea. Something you connect to only from the outside can affect you only superficially.

When you understand the depth of an idea, you see that it contains a truth that relates to every aspect of your life and the world. Its meaning and value grow, because it is not about one case: you can apply it to every case and carry it for the rest of your life.

The more deeply you analyze something, the more personally meaningful it becomes, and the more likely you are to keep thinking about it and remember it. Connected to this is abstraction: the more abstract the point you find in an idea, the more widely it applies. Seeing only the one thing gives it less value.

blocks.title: Teaching someone to fish
blocks.text: Compare someone who gives you a fish: you eat it and it is gone. Someone who teaches you to fish gives you something that stays with you for life.

The *haavaras ayin* is a passing glance, the way someone just sees something. The *tviyas ayin* is the imprint of the eye: an expert looks at something and every detail carries meaning, because of their earlier study and understanding. The more understanding you have, the better you separate the signal from the noise, see what is relevant and zero in on what is essential and how it connects.

phrases.he: וכן העברת עין השכל
phrases.en: the same thing applies if a person's mind's eye

phrases.he: באיזה סברא בהשקפה ראשונה
phrases.en: So, just like when you physically see something, there's a big difference between just looking at it quickly, or if you show it to somebody that's not an expert versus if you show it to an expert that really has that appreciation

phrases.he: בלתי עכוב והעמדה לעיין בו היטב,
phrases.en: On the other, in the same way with the mind's eye, where you're not looking at something physical, if you just let an idea wash over your mind and don't stop to really dwell on it and think about it and pull it apart

phrases.he: ולא ידע בסברא זו לתכליתה כלל
phrases.en: you're not going to really know and understand the depth of that idea at all

blocks.text: The same goes for the mind's eye. As with the physical eye, there is a big difference between a quick look and a look from someone who is not an expert, and a look from an expert who spends the time to really look at it and examine it.

With the mind's eye you are not looking at something physical but at an idea, comparing it to your own self-perception. If you let an idea wash over your mind and don't stop to dwell on it, pull it apart and think about it, you will not know its depth at all.

The Rambam says of the teachings of the Sages that there are three groups. The first understands them simply and believes them simply. The second also understands them simply, and says they are not true. The third, which is hardly a group at all, sees that there is real depth there, and takes the time and effort to plumb it and find the true wisdom behind the statements in the Talmud and the Midrash.

Take the simplest talk everybody hears at the Shabbos table and mine it. Learn it once. Then learn it again and write a point-by-point summary. Then think about the summary: what is the real theme, what is the main topic, what is the paradigm shift, how did I look at it before and how will I look at it after, what examples of that shift are there in my life, and what would it mean if I made it?

Mining takes about as long as learning the thing three times, not much longer than learning it once. In that time a nice saying turns into something life-changing that you carry forever. It is a good investment: in the same time you could learn three things at a low level and soon forget them, or spend the time on one thing that stays valuable forever. That is the kind of learning Chabad wants.

blocks.title: The eighth day of Pesach
blocks.text: The Rebbe explains at length that the eighth day of Pesach is the day that stands above the seven. He says he will have to leave soon, and this is what he wants to say before he goes.

The Rebbe's final takeaway is connecting to G-dliness for its own sake, apart from creation. The practical point: every person should commit to setting aside time at least once a week to think about an idea in Chassidus. Not to prepare for a class or for something later, just to connect to G-d and make these ideas part of himself.

That is much of what Chabad is about, and it is work, which is why it is called *avoda*. It takes effort, but the extra effort to mine an idea is what gets the diamonds. Without it you get only the dirt on the surface, or a piece of coal lying around.

blocks.text: The last class set up the question: why can't you get away with learning an idea once, why must you go through this process? The answer comes in the next part: every idea has a depth, a length and a width, and the depth cannot be reached without going through the length and the width.

blocks.question: Does this apply to permanence of perception? People come back from a vacation moved by a natural sight and feel it was a kind of spiritual experience, but does it last?

blocks.text: To get something that lasts and really changes a person takes this process. A passing inspiration from seeing nature is not enough; it has to be deliberate and thoughtful.

sections.title: Depth, length and width: the three dimensions of every idea
sections.summary: Every idea has depth, length and width. Width is the many explanations, length brings the idea down to something tangible, and depth is the essential point from which the rest flows.

phrases.he: כי הנה ג' דברים הוא שיש בכל דבר מושכל.
phrases.en: that every idea has these three parts, three dimensions

phrases.he: עומק ואורך ורוחב.
phrases.en: There's the depth, the length, and the width.

blocks.text: Every idea has three parts: the depth, the length and the width. To arrive at the depth you have to go through the length and the width; you cannot get the depth immediately. That is why you need this process of study, *iyun* and *hisbonenus*, to get to the depth.

phrases.he: הרוחב הוא בחינת הסבר המושכל
phrases.en: he says the width is explaining an idea

phrases.he: לכל צד בפרטים הרבה
phrases.en: with all its details, all of its what he calls, like, to each side, the elaboration of the idea

phrases.he: כרוחב הנהר, ולא דברים כהווייתן לבד, כנהר קצר.
phrases.en: and not just giving like a simple kind of like dictionary definition, which would be like a narrow river

blocks.text: *Rochav*, the width, is explaining an idea in many details, to each side, like the width of a river. It is not the bare definition, the narrow river of a dictionary entry. Seeing the same idea in many examples and many of its parts gives breadth of experience and breadth of explanation. That is the width.

blocks.text: The length is how far the idea descends into concrete metaphors, so that it reaches the understanding of a small child. Bring it all the way down and it becomes tangible, physical, sensory. That is the length.

blocks.title: A river that comes down to you
blocks.text: An idea is like a river that flows down from the mountain to the low countryside. You do not have to climb the mountain to get the water; it comes down to you.

He says this is explained at length in the manuscripts, about the *orech hayeriah*. He is not sure what manuscripts means here: it can mean any Chassidic discourses, or the longer discourses of the Alter Rebbe from late in his life, which were called manuscripts. He thinks it refers to those, and that some discourses explain this idea.

The big problem in teaching an abstract subject like math, or any science, is skipping the first step: bringing it down to something that is intuitive daily experience. Word problems about little Timmy going to a candy shop, or a plane with a tailwind, are not practical, so they do not really help.

blocks.text: He takes his own work in education as the example. If he were designing something to teach kids math, he would build a game around working in a store, starting as a low-level employee and moving up as you get good at things. First you fill orders and take money and give change, which is addition and subtraction. Then you pack an order into the fewest boxes, say thirteen items with boxes that hold four and five, which is the basis of division and multiplication. The intuition comes first, and the math follows from it.

blocks.text: The same is true of most subjects. Look at how people came to a skill: when they only need basic transactions, addition and subtraction are enough. When they buy packages of eggs, multiplication appears, and dividing into cartons is division. Once the real need is there, you wish for a tool, and then the tool is easy to learn. Stay grounded in real experience and in the real problems that made the tool necessary. You can get by counting on your fingers until you wish you had symbols for counting on your toes and your friend's.

blocks.title: The depth of a river
blocks.text: The depth of an idea is like the depth of a river. The river's depth is not itself wide; it is the source from which the river spreads out. Its real essence is the stream, the undercurrent: slow water fills the riverbed around it, but in the centre runs a pipeline of water that moves quickly. The real essence of a river is that flow from its source.

Water on top of the depth and at its sides is secondary to it. When the volume of water overflows, it spreads to the sides, making width, and height, and it extends along the whole length of the flow. But the main thing is the volume of water that is moving.

phrases.he: כך עומק המושכל הוא בחינת עצם נקודתו כמו שהוא,
phrases.en: And so too, the depth of an idea. In other words, the real essence of any idea is that it's coming from somewhere

phrases.he: ונקרא עומק המושג
phrases.en: and so this depth of idea is called the *omek hamusag*, the depth of the grasp

blocks.text: So too, the depth of an idea is its essence as it is: the point it comes from. The real essence of any idea is that it is coming from somewhere, connected to a fundamental source, the way water flows from its source. Everything else is examples.

blocks.title: Teaching a child the color red
blocks.text: Teach a small child the color red: show him a red apple, a red car, a red book, until he has enough breadth of experience. You are not explaining the wavelength of light or how the eye works. It is something you can point to and say, that's red. Once he has that breadth, he can begin to appreciate the depth of it.
The depth is the fundamental point, which is abstract, and every example is that same point applied in a slightly different way. When a person grasps that point, he grasps the depth of the idea.

That is how anything is taught: first give a tangible experience, the more concrete and personal the better, because if it is too abstract the learner cannot relate to it. With enough such experiences, which is the width, he can generalize and get the abstract essence. That generalization is the depth. That is how you learn anything.

This depth is called *omek hamusag*, the depth of the grasp of the concept. Whatever spreads out in length, width and height comes from that essential point. For a teacher who has mastered the idea, the fundamental concept already includes all the explanations and examples he will give. They are the same point, given in different examples and applied in different ways.

blocks.title: Adding apples, then fifths
blocks.text: Teach a child to add: one apple plus one apple is two apples, until he can relate to it. Once he can abstract that, he can add anything, and it is fundamentally the same thing again and again, whether apples or fractions. One fifth plus one fifth is two fifths: the same idea.

A more fundamental point lets you build more complexity. That complexity comes from doing the simple things and packaging more of them together, layer by layer. Multiplication is adding many times, and an exponent is multiplying many times.

In Chassidus, the *Frierdiker Rebbe* gives an example of this, with height built from depth. He says that one of Moshiach's main accomplishments is that even *tzaddikim* will do *teshuva*, and that Chassidus knows *teshuva* does not only mean repenting for a sin, so it applies even to a *tzaddik*. There are two paths in the service of G-d: a *tzaddik*'s approach is from above downward, and a *baal teshuva*'s is from below upward. The human intellect cannot naturally see how they differ, since either way you must be a vessel for the light. So he offers a tangible *mashal*.

blocks.title: Raw and cooked food
blocks.text: Some food, such as fruit and vegetables, can be eaten raw, and cooking it adds only a little to its flavor. Other food, like meat and fish, is dangerous raw and must be cooked thoroughly until what was dangerous is edible and delicious. The difference is between something already fit to eat, where a little work brings out what is there, and something bad that you must work on to make useful.

A *tzaddik*'s *avoda* is mainly about what is already holy: *Torah* and *mitzvos* that are already G-dly. Even without *kavana* you are doing a G-dly thing and it is a *mitzva*; *kavana* only enhances it. The light is already there, and what is needed is the vessel.

The *baal teshuva*'s *avoda* is the opposite: taking what is mundane in a person's nature and the world, which tends to be bad, and using it for the sake of Heaven. That takes more work and is more of an accomplishment. The depth is the same in both; understanding it in one context lets you climb and see it higher. That is building the height.

The height is only possible because he first brought the idea down to something very tangible that we can all relate to. Once we grasp it there and find its depth, we can climb to a higher level of abstraction and appreciate it in a more spiritual form.

sections.title: Height and the wellspring: the depth above, and binah as the river of chachma
sections.summary: Going higher from the depth reaches the depth above, which he ties to the flood of Noach and the Zohar. Bina is the river and chachma its wellspring, and learning any idea runs through all three dimensions.

blocks.text: Back to the parentheses. The idea goes higher and higher until it reaches the *omek rom*, the depth of above. That is basically the revelation of G-d's essence, the highest perception of G-dliness, like the water that rose higher and higher in the flood of Noach.

The Zohar says there will be a spiritual flood in the times of *Moshiach*, similar to the flood of *Noach*. *Noach* represents the *middah* of *yesod*, which stands for the sixth millennium, and his 600th year is the 600th year of that millennium, which he believes is 1840. That was the beginning of the flooding of the knowledge of *Chassidus* and the knowledge of the sciences. The Zohar says the wells of wisdom will be opened, the wells of the abyss, which are two kinds of knowledge.

The water from below is the knowledge of the physical world and the sciences. It climbs higher and higher until it covers the mountains, and as our appreciation of what we see in the physical world is refined, it eventually reaches up to G-dliness and meets the upper waters.

Then the wellsprings from above open, to bring down the water above the heavens, the upper depth, which depends on the lower depth. Reb Hillel Paritcher explains that this depends on bittul and humility, which make a person a vessel for the upper depth, and on a simple faith that recognizes something is beyond us and that we have no knowledge of our own.

That faith is the foundation, like the matzah we have just eaten at Pesach. With it a person can understand the deepest things of G-dliness; that is why at the giving of the Torah we were able to receive the whole essence of the Torah. Seeing G-dliness through physical mitzvos and the physical world leads to the highest understanding philosophy can reach. The depth of an idea can only be reached through physical experience, the one place where its essence is found. Learning afterwards helps unpack it; without the experience it is just words.

Because the beginning is wedged in the end, G-d's real desire and essence is found in the lowest thing, the physical world, in doing physical mitzvos. Cast your question down to the depth, or raise it up above: by starting with that lower depth, you take your question down, and then you can raise it up and have the perception of these high spiritual truths.

The Mitteler Rebbe talks about this a lot, and elsewhere in *Shaar HaEmuna*, which is printed together with this one: first a foundation of simple faith and of doing, before hearing, and within understanding too. When we think about G-dliness, it all has to focus on seeing it in the physical world, seeing how things are created from nothing. If a person only thinks about abstract ideas, he will never really get to the depth of seeing G-dliness.

So all the length, the width and everything else of the idea come from that essential point, where it flows from *chachma*. That is called *ayin*, the abstract essence of the idea, the abstract point. Like it says, a river flowed out of Eden.

phrases.he: שהבינה נקרא נהר
phrases.en: And this is the idea that *bina* is called a river

phrases.he: והחכמה נקרא מעיין,
phrases.en: and its source is in *chachma*, which is called the *maayan*, called a wellspring

phrases.he: כידוע

blocks.text: *Bina* is called a river and *chachma* its wellspring, as is known. This is the image for the whole discussion.

Every idea has three parts: length, width and depth. We are aiming at the depth, the real essential understanding, the inner point, which is abstract and general, so that it applies in all kinds of situations and examples. It can be seen physically and spiritually, as a central theme that flows through everything. But to arrive at it we first need the length and the width.

That is the basic idea of the process of learning this, and of learning anything. We need the quality of the experience first. Then seeing the same thing in many diverse things lets us tell what is essential from what is circumstantial, and unpack it to the inner core of the idea.

In simple terms: learn one discourse and try to understand it clearly, then learn another, and compare them to see the central theme that runs through both. In this book we will learn a number of meshalim, say five metaphors for one idea, and see the common theme that unites them, how they differ, how the idea changes when it is applied to different situations, and what stays the same.

blocks.question: If a person masters a concept intellectually, shouldn't it reach his emotions and his actions too? If he understands it but does not feel connected to it emotionally, hasn't he missed its essence?
blocks.text: Yes. When you really understand these things, it is intellectually enlightening and personally relevant, which gives a strong emotional connection, love and fear, and so it changes your actions. We are not learning math. We are learning who we are and what our mission in the world is. If we really get it, we live it and feel it, so *haskala* and *avoda* must be one thing.

So you have to put in the extra work, sometimes a lot, to mine an idea: what is it really saying, how do I see it in my life, what is the paradigm shift from how I looked at it before, and how would that change how I act in these situations. Then start to try it out.

blocks.title: Learning to swim
blocks.text: It is like teaching someone to swim who is terrified of the water. You can talk until you are blue in the face, but he will not change how he feels until he gets in the water and sees that he can be in control. It is the same with these ideas: understand them, then see them in practice in your life.
You need to understand it and then see it in practice to get a real, deep change of perspective: to see that it works, that this is who you are, and then it clicks and becomes the way you see things.

The class opens by going back over lines 9 to 16. Length is the first step in learning anything: a person needs an experience he can have directly, something tangible and not just words. Then come diverse experiences, which must be analysed for what stays the same and what changes, and that gives the depth: the fundamental principles. The depth comes from *chachma*, and *bina* is the river that flows from it, like the river that comes out of Eden.

sections.title: Iyun: slow study past one's comfort, the vessel for the depth of bina
sections.summary: *Iyun* is the slow, repeated study that goes past what a reader already knows and is comfortable with. It is the vessel through which *bina* reaches its depth, not the 'depth of daas' that the world means by the phrase.

blocks.text: *Iyun* is going through the length and the width of an idea to reach its depth. The dwelling and the analysis have to go past what the reader already knows and is comfortable with. Every idea comes in the shell of its tangible form, and natural intuition does not get through that shell to the abstract essence beneath it. So a person pushes until he finds things that surprise him and go beyond the way he would naturally see them.

*Iyun* is also patience: a person must spend more time with an idea than he would naturally want to. That is the *yegiat basar* and *yegiat nefesh*, the toil of the flesh and the toil of the soul: sitting and being more patient than one feels like, and delving deeper than intuition would make one comfortable.

Arriving at the depth means finding the real abstract point, one that applies to all cases and not only to one. Story structure, which he had recently been reading about, is an example: one of the main ideas is that a story is not about what happens but about how what happens transforms the character. Inherent to a story is a character with a misbelief about reality, and the events force him to confront it and learn something. That is a deep idea, not apparent at first, which comes from delving in. This is the depth of an idea in its inner essence, deep to its core.

blocks.text: To look at something with the eye, as the line says, is not to pass over it with a passing glance. It is to scrutinize it with a trained, discerning eye, letting the details sink in.

The line describes a long look, the way the Frierdiker Rebbe describes a craftsman who takes something apart and sets each piece aside. He checks each piece: is it in good condition, can it be fixed, or must it be discarded? Only after evaluating all the pieces, and seeing how the whole comes apart and goes together, can he plan the repair and the reassembly. An educator analysing a student does the same: he pulls apart the student's nature, habits, environment, and good and bad qualities, judges each one, and then sees how they fit the whole and sets priorities. Only then does a person understand a thing in all its details and inner workings.
blocks.title: The craftsman who takes it apart

blocks.text: The word *hisbonenus* is spelled with a double *nun*, which grammatically implies doing the thing again and again: intense study. Had it been *girsa*, it would have one *nun*. Rashi glosses *iyun* as dwelling on a thing until one understands it clearly.

So we cannot be satisfied with the basic idea, or with being able to repeat it back like a parrot. We have to train ourselves to want the gold nugget, the diamond at the core: something more abstract and more universal, relevant far beyond this one case. It is a real paradigm shift for everything.

blocks.text: *Iyun* is only a vessel, a tool, for reaching the depth of *bina* itself. The mind has two powers. One is the ability to appreciate an abstract concept, which is the real depth of the idea. To get there you need to hold the idea in the mind with its external details, so that it can be grasped.

Picture a nut. First you get a firm grasp on it, which is the length: holding the idea in the mind. Then you split it open, which is the width: analysing the differences between one place and another. Only then can you reach in and get at the kernel, which is the depth.
blocks.title: Cracking a nut

blocks.text: The world calls this *iyun* *amkus hadaas*, which people translate as just focus. That is not so: *amkus hadaas* is only a vessel, not the depth of the matter itself.

The teacher was taught that focusing on the idea is the external vessel. Reb Hillel Paritcher reverses this: analysis gives the basic understanding, and *amkus hadaas* comes when a person connects to the idea personally and finds its relevance to himself, which takes him into *chachma*.
Motivation is part of it, but more, it lets you empathize with the idea. You find the idea inside yourself and identify with it, and then you can generalize it to a much greater degree.
blocks.question: Is the relevance to our own interests what motivates us to keep comparing and contrasting, even when it is frustrating?

blocks.text: They could be the same. The depth is abstract and more general. You can tell somebody the words that represent the depth, but they will not understand it. A person has the depth when he appreciates that abstract generalization in a rich way and sees how it applies to things.
blocks.question: When we say depth, is the difference between what we are calling the abstract and the depth the same thing?

blocks.text: The example is the hero's journey, a theme that underlies stories, which he had recently seen. A person can be told the idea, and then think about it in the context of his own life and how his experiences transformed him. When he sees in himself that he has his own misbeliefs, and how experiences lead him to uncover them and reach a more accurate, more mature understanding of himself and the world, he can see the same in other people. The essential struggle and journey is the same for everybody, and that is why there is something universal in that kind of story.
blocks.title: A misbelief in one's own life

blocks.text: Yes. We are going from *bina* to *chachma*. There is the depth of *bina*, and then there is *chachma*.
blocks.question: So is that the meaning of 'to the depth of the matter itself', as opposed to the regular depth: the abstract point, which applies universally?

sections.title: Chachma: the wellspring has its own depth, and the chachma within bina
sections.summary: *Chachma* is the flash of a new idea and the abstract essence that comes before any system. It is a wellspring with its own depth, length and width, and reaching its depth activates the *bina* within it, so that a person can explain one idea in many ways.

blocks.text: The teacher gives an example from arithmetic. *Chachma* is the axiom: the basic perspective one must accept before building a logical system on it. Take one plus one equals two. It seems plain common sense, but it rests on assumptions, on a philosophy of commodities in which each unit is the same as the next and we care only how many there are. When you buy and sell apples, each one stays a unit, and then you group them in a basket. That is where one plus one is two comes from.
blocks.title: One plus one is two

blocks.text: Mix red and blue and you do not get two; you get a third thing, a synthesis. If the world were blobs of mud without distinct edges, or if we were talking about people marrying, where one plus one and then the children does not equal two, that logic would not make sense. The symbols express a logic, and the logic rests on a way of looking at the world and on priorities: which aspects of a thing we focus on. That is why we are not allowed to count people in a census. Treating a person as a number is dehumanizing, because it says that only how many there are matters.

blocks.text: So there is *chachma*: a belief system, a philosophy or way of looking at the world, which is the real depth behind the system you create. Change those basic assumptions and all the rules change. Regular Euclidean geometry against non-Euclidean geometry is the example, and the Rebbe gives it too. Morality works the same way: you can build a whole legal system on assumptions, and when two reasonable people differ on what is the higher priority and what matters, they reach very different conclusions. That perspective and those values are the *chachma*; the whole logic built to express them is *bina*.

blocks.text: When you keep asking why, you eventually reach a point where you cannot answer any more, and the answer is that it is just the way it is, or that it is the assumption we are making. Arriving there, at the presuppositions or axioms, is arriving at *chachma*: finding the core concept behind everything.

blocks.text: Richard Feynman, as a boy, pulled a wagon with a ball in it, and when he pulled it the ball rolled to the back. He asked his father why, and his father said, 'Oh, inertia.' What is inertia? That is what scientists call the fact that the ball rolls to the back of the wagon. What turned him on was seeing that with such simple questions about everyday things you can quickly reach the edge of human knowledge. Why does what you throw up fall? Gravity. What is gravity? That is what we call the fact that things fall.

blocks.text: Real understanding at the level of *chachma* is what is technically called metacognition: a person becomes aware of the assumptions he is making, and sees that his logic holds because of this assumption and perspective, and could differ from another. In a *pilpul* in the Gemara, a question can have no answer unless you look at it from a different perspective.

blocks.text: Tosafos's question on Rashi is based on Tosafos looking at the whole thing from a slightly different perspective. From Tosafos's perspective there is no answer; you have to answer it from Rashi's perspective. You learn to recognise that they look at it slightly differently, which is why one says it one way and the other the other way. Being aware of those differences is the level of *chachma*.

blocks.text: Yes, that is the key. When you reach the level of *chachma*, the sign that you are reaching that depth is that the two ways of looking at it are mutually exclusive. They are both valid, but they cannot be done at the same time.

A system is a rough description of one aspect of reality when you look at it this way, but it is not the whole thing. You can choose to look at it one way when that is useful and another way when that is useful, but neither is really the whole picture.

blocks.text: A listener reports learning that day in *Shaar HaEmuna* that one should daven with the eyes down and the heart up. There are two ways of contemplating. One is to stir the G-dly soul alone; that leaves the heart below in the physical world, and the animal soul is not changed, so when a person goes back to the world it all goes away. The other is to focus on seeing G-dliness in the world, in ways the animal soul can understand and appreciate. That changes the animal soul and wakes the G-dly soul too, so the two connect and it lasts. This connects to the point that *hisbonenus* starts in *bina* and from there reaches *chachma*.

blocks.text: *Chachma* is the abstract essence of the idea, before it reaches the depth of the concept that is in *bina*. The relation is that of the spring to the river: the spring is the source, and from it the river flows out.

Depth at the root of an idea: when a person delves into the depth of *bina* in one particular case and understands it very well, that gives him an insight into the higher depth automatically, which is *chachma*.

That depth is called the depth of *chachma*, or its hidden *taalumos chachma*. *Bina* has length, width and depth, called *yesh*: the concrete example you are studying. In the same way *chachma* has its own length, width and depth, called *ayin*, the abstract.

blocks.text: The depth of the spring is like the levels in *bina*. For any topic, *chachma* is developing a person's intuition into the depth of the idea and having a clearer grasp of its assumptions and axioms, which is metacognition. Within *chachma* itself a person can develop a stronger, deeper appreciation of it.

What is the depth of a spring? It is the source, the underground aquifer where the water comes from. From there it spreads out and rises until it breaks through the surface, coming out in drops from its hiddenness. The deeper the source is under the ground, the more hidden it is.
blocks.title: The source of a spring

blocks.text: Like the springs of the deep that burst forth in Noach's flood, the earth is riddled with veins of water, and veins of oil, gold and natural gas: hidden reservoirs of potential under the ground, each with a first depth.
blocks.title: Veins under the ground

blocks.text: A person has the same kind of untapped potential in the mind, to understand things in new ways and to have creative ideas. Each idea is one drip coming out of that source, and if a person learns to mine it, he can extract all kinds of new things.

It says that *chachma* comes from *ayin*, from nothing. Even though *chachma* is the beginning of a thought, the first flash of a new idea, it has a first source deeper than itself: the hidden source called the depth of *chachma*.

So, as with *bina*, where the idea has its depth and this particular explanation or application only applies that depth, *chachma* has its real source. It is one particular way of expressing that source, and one can delve deeper.

On the simplest level, *chachma* is coming up with a new idea. It seems that a person cannot actively invent, but a person can learn to reach in and find the real source of those ideas and change their assumptions, so that they come out differently. The big part of this is metacognition: becoming aware of your assumptions and your process, and looking at things from a new angle. Analysing an existing story to understand the author's intention is the depth of *bina*. Creating a new story, or a genre that never existed before, is where a new approach comes from.
blocks.question: Once you already have the broader message behind the stories, what would the depth of *chachma* be, and what is a practical example of going from the depth of *bina* to the depth of *chachma* in real subjects?

blocks.text: Abstracting the axioms from the explanations is one step. Changing the axioms themselves, which gives a totally different insight into the subject, is another.

Mathematics is one facet, and there are other ways of quantifying data. Mastering addition as it is taught is the depth of *bina*. Being able to talk about the assumptions behind it, and change them consciously, is the depth of *chachma*: 1+1=2 is not inherently true, and with different axioms you get totally different mathematics. Some people have insights into what inventors made. The inventors themselves can change their assumptions at will, while others have to wait for a new idea.

blocks.text: *Chachma* is the idea of getting a new idea, which comes like a flash of lightning. One would think of it as something that comes from above, like a muse who visits and cannot be chosen. But it really has depth, so a person can open up those new ideas.
The source of that flash is its hidden depth, which is its real essence and its inner source: the source of a person's ability to have a new idea.

Like we said, the depth of *bina* is only the depth of a concrete understanding, a particular logical explanation that can be clearly defined in a revealed logic. Its depth is the abstract essence of that concrete *yesh*.

Compared with *chachma* before it has been developed into systems, the depth of *bina* has no relationship to it. One *chachma* can be explained in many systems of logic, and that is *bina*. So even the depth of one system is small and tangible next to how general and abstract *chachma* is.

Take addition. We use base ten, computers use binary, and some systems use hexadecimal, with sixteen digits. They look very different on the outside, and teaching children to add in binary would be a different curriculum. But certain fundamentals are the same in a certain way: only the way it is expressed differs.

blocks.text: The same is true of how Rashi and Tosafos explain one idea in different ways, with different reasons. They don't necessarily disagree. Sometimes it is a totally different perspective; sometimes it is the same thing explained with a different logic or from a different angle. And even the depth of *bina* cannot compare to *chachma*, which is its essence.

blocks.text: The depth of the concept is called the *shaar hanun* of *bina*. Although it is drawn from the *ayin* of *chachma* into *yesh*, it is already one particular concrete example. Like the prophecy that when *Moshiach* comes, a river will start flowing from the Holy of Holies in the *Beis HaMikdash*, starting as narrow as the horn of a grasshopper.
Its source is in *Keser*, and *chachma* is in the *kodesh kodashim*. It only becomes a river when it leaves the *kodesh kodashim* and goes out into expression in the outside world.

The Mitteler Rebbe gives this explanation of how it works in learning any idea, the relation between *chachma* and *bina*. The point is the study of how G-dliness is expressed in the physical world, the *yichuda tata'a* and creation *yesh me'ayin*, set against the appreciation of the G-dly soul, which sees the *yichuda ila'a*, a far more spiritual appreciation of G-dliness.
Whatever *hisbonenus* we do on the physical world seems so limited and tangible next to the vast sea of *chachma*, which is much more abstract. In a way it is.

In any subject you can philosophise forever about ways to look at it, but once you limit yourself to one system it is very particular and limited, with idiosyncrasies that are not fundamental to the field. Take someone in technology who learns one language or one technology: it brings many specific skills and quirks, and it could be done another way. Yet when you really master one such system, you start to appreciate the fundamentals that are the same in any system, because it still contains that nugget of *chachma*.
blocks.title: Learning one system well

blocks.text: That is the point of the root reaching up: the depth of *bina* reaches not only to *chachma* but to its depth, all the way to *Keser*, the real source of *chachma*. So when a person does *hisbonenus* on the external details alone, that too activates and opens the depth of *chachma* and gives the ability to invent new insights into that deeper level.

The Rebbe Rashab wrote books for his students in *Tomchei Temimim* on how to learn *Gemara* and how to learn *Chassidus*. He says not to try to come up with a *chidush*. Learn the text to understand it very clearly, and learn it about five times: once quickly for the basic idea, again for the flow, again to really understand it, then review it a few times until it is clear and solid.

Also learn from more than one source. Learn the Gemara; then learn how Rashi understands it until that is clear; then learn how Tosafos understands it until that is clear; then contrast the two and see where they agree and disagree, and why.

When you understand the idea clearly from Rashi's perspective and from Tosafos's, that gives a deeper understanding, the depth of *bina*. From doing that you eventually open the depth of *chachma* too: you see the deeper underlying pattern, and later you find that the text says it somewhere else. The same in *Chassidus*: learn the way it is explained in one *ma'amar* of the Mitteler Rebbe and in one of the *Tzemach Tzedek*, or take more than one *mashal* for the same idea.

After that you find new insights you were not taught, and you find you had the correct understanding of the general principles all along. The Rebbe says elsewhere, *Baruch shekivanti*: I got it right.

This process, of activating the depth of *chachma* and gaining new insights beyond what you were taught, is called *me'ameik*. Compared with *iyun*, which digs down to the source of a well, *me'ameik* is a verb that causes something else to get deeper. You do not dig the well yourself; you cause it to activate.

Learn the Gemara properly with Rashi's and Tosafos's opinions, and you get a deep understanding that lets you come up with your own explanation and see the fundamental principles and how they apply. The same in *Chassidus*, or in any subject: if a person really tries to understand the fundamental assumptions of a subject, he will recognise where he could change some of them and look at it differently, and be inventive.

I didn't hear that, but maybe. It is similar: when you appreciate the depth of one perspective and of another, you need that triangulation, which is the width. And when you get to the depth of contrasting things, it opens up something much deeper than the understanding of each.

blocks.text: In our service we explain G-dliness to the animal soul, in a way it can understand physically in the world. That activates the connection of the G-dly soul too. If we try to focus only on activating the G-dly soul, it does not affect the animal soul, and it leaves us disconnected: whatever we accomplish in davening evaporates. So everything should be focused and grounded in the physical world and in these tangible examples. That automatically develops the spiritual sensitivity and wakes the G-dly soul, which is in a way much deeper and more powerful, but it is better for many reasons to do it this way.

blocks.text: The line says this is explained in the Chassidic manuscripts. The teacher thinks it is a quotation from *Sefer Yetzirah*, though he is not sure. The idea is *ayin-bet* within *samech-gimel*: the *chachma* of *bina* and the *bina* of *chachma*. The name *ayin-bet* is a spelling of the Name that relates to *chachma*.

The spelling out, *milui*: each letter is written out in full, so *yud* is written *yud-vav-dalet*, and each combination has a different numerical value. Four such spellings are discussed in *Kabbalah*: the Names of 72, 63, 45 and 52, which correspond to *chachma*, *bina*, the *middos*, and *Malchus*. One can also have a *milui* of a *milui*, spelling it out further.
*Eitz Chaim* has a whole section on the sparks that came down in the breaking of the vessels, and it calculates how they relate to the levels of these Names when they are spelled out.
blocks.title: Eitz Chaim and the sparks

blocks.text: For our purposes, this is *chachma* within *bina*: the *ayin-bet* within *samech-gimel*, which is the idea of being wise within your understanding. It means you do not understand the idea only at its surface, but delve until you reach the abstract point that is its essence. That is the *iyun* that reaches the depth of *bina*.

The new insight stays within the concept being understood in *bina*. You do not apply it to a new topic or outside its field or natural place; you get new insights there. If you learn a page of Gemara, you may find a new way to understand it, a new explanation of Rashi or Tosafos, or an answer to a question, but within the idea you are learning. A true realization comes only through *iyun*.

In practice: study it until it is very clear, comparing why it says this here and that there. Then make a bullet-point summary of what you learned. Once that is clear, arrange the information into categories and see how the points line up. Find the relationships and comparisons between ideas, the ones that relate and the ones that contrast, and the different opinions, and analyse the data. Once you do that, you will see new ideas and relationships that were not immediately apparent.
That process of studying the idea and getting all its pieces clear in front of you, without trying for a new idea, is *iyun* itself, and it is called *bina sheb'bina*: *bina* within *bina*.

From there a person can invent new ideas and be creative, coming up with a new understanding and a new explanation, but only within the same topic. That new insight within what you are learning is called *chachma sheb'bina*. Explaining it a different way, arranging it differently, and finding comparisons and parallels within what you are learning is having *chachma* within *bina*.

The *Keser* of *bina* is the real depth of the concept, the source of both, and it means connecting to the essence of the idea, which is your real *bittul* to it. That reaches beyond *bina* all the way to the essence of *chachma* too.
The *shaar nun* of *bina*, the real essence of one's understanding, reaches all the way up to the depth of *chachma* and can activate totally new understanding.

This can be generalised to something abstract that applies far beyond the field you are learning. You see connections between math, music and literature in secular studies, or in learning Gemara, between one *sugya* in *Sukkah* and something in *Bava Metzia*, though they are not the same topic.

The Rebbe famously explains the approach of *Beis Hillel* against *Beis Shammai*, and how that approach runs through many topics. There are running themes behind the approach of *Rabbi Shimon* against *Rabbi Yehuda*. This is discussed in many places in the Rebbe's *sichos* and in other talks, and the Ragatchover Gaon often does it too.

Seeing broader ideas, a general assumption or approach that applies to many topics, is reaching this level of *chachma*. Once you find it, you see it is not only something in one idea of Torah; it relates to life, a general idea you can look at life through. They call these big ideas.

In curriculum design they recommend an approach called *Understanding by Design*, which asks you to identify the big ideas and big questions in any subject. Understanding is defined as being able to generalise what you learn to those bigger ideas and questions beyond the immediate topic. Read a story about the Pilgrims, and ask what themes and struggles they faced, and where we find them in our lives or other times in history.
blocks.title: Big ideas in curriculum design

blocks.text: In our *hisbonenus* what we want is to take what we experience in a mitzvah and see that approach in everything in life, *bechol drachecha deihu*. When we contemplate one aspect of creation, such as G-d giving life through food, or waking up in the morning, we see that the experience is an example of a much deeper, general G-dly idea: a little taste of the infinite, which we can experience in everything we see. More on this later, in the *yichudim*. That is the *chachma* within *bina*.

blocks.text: *Bina* within *chachma*, the *samech-gimel* of *ayin-bet*: this is the power of explanation within *chachma* itself. Once a person has the deeper approach of *chachma*, he can bring the idea into many explanations. Without that depth, one gets a new way of looking at something now and then, but *chachma* does not extend into *bina*, the *bina* within *chachma*.

With the depth of *chachma* they have access to this *bina* of *chachma*: they can at will explain the idea in many ways, change their perspective, and so explain it to a different person, apply it to a different situation, or give a different *mashal*. That is an open creativity in how the idea is expressed.

Yes, generally that is the idea. To zero in on the difference when crossing the boundary, take number theory, as we talked about last time. Everyone learns arithmetic and multiplication tables and takes the decimal system's assumptions for granted. You can master that system, find new ways of doing the multiplication, and learn tricks and shortcuts. Those are *chachma* within *bina*: new ways of mastering the system.
blocks.question: Is the difference like studying a packet of papers from a teacher, where the insights into its different facets are *chachma* of *bina*? Once you have looked at it from every angle and got to its depth, you can explain it in all sorts of ways, and use different analogies for a friend who relates to cars or sports?

blocks.text: Why was this system invented? People counted with tally marks, then grouped them, with a slash through every five, so that the number could be seen quickly. Then came Roman numerals, with a symbol for ones, another for fives and another for tens, which made it easier to see the number but still needed adding up, and new symbols for each bigger number. Then the decimal system, which uses the same ten digits over and over.

In the decimal system the order matters: each move over multiplies by ten. Tally and Roman systems do not depend much on order. The decimal is just one system, and there were others. Computers use binary, and base eight or base twelve can make the mathematics easier at times.

When you understand the *Keser*, the real motivation and desire, the design goal of why the system exists (to count and do commerce easily), then you understand its assumptions and their advantages, and you can think consciously about other bases or a different system altogether. It is like a consultant designing from scratch for someone: you want to know what they really want to accomplish, and choose the assumptions and system that best serve them. That mastery is completely different from being a student.

The same holds in programming. Someone who leads a project should know many technologies and choose the right ones for the work. Someone with a bag of tricks and fifty ways to do a thing can rank them against the customer's needs, and sometimes there is an objectively better way. Doing everything the one way you know is often less efficient. But it is also hard to find people who can freely choose and design from scratch, and it is not always worth reinventing the wheel when the developers already know a technology. So you weigh the technical advantages against the learning curve.
blocks.title: Choosing the right technology

blocks.text: Yes. The main spiritual thing this level of *chachma*, especially the *bina* of *chachma*, opens up is *bittul*. A person with *bittul* and *emuna*, in the simplest sense, will accept whatever G-d sends, whether he understands it or not, and do what he is told because he trusts it is meant to be done.
blocks.question: Could that be applied to life, so that a person asks why G-d put his soul into a physical body, what His design goal was in having him interact with Him in this way?

blocks.text: A person who develops this deeper essence becomes aware of G-d's real intention, which is not only beyond us but something we can be aware of. So we have the *bina* of *chachma*: we see the G-dly purpose in whatever situation we are in and participate in it actively. When we do something openly holy, like a mitzvah, we appreciate how we serve G-d in it. When we have to go out into the world and deal with darkness, we see that G-dliness is there too, and not limited to that circumstance. The person gets the message behind the experience, looks past its superficial form, and says: there is something deeper here.

The famous story is of Reb Zusha and Reb Elimelech in prison. They could not daven, because there is poop in the corner, and from a Jewish legal standpoint they cannot pray there. One of them was sad, and was told that by not praying they were following the law, which pleases G-d. They realised that nothing in a dungeon can stop them from deepening their relationship with G-d, and they started dancing. A guard asked what was making them happy. Another inmate told the officer they were pointing at the poop and dancing. The officer said: if that's what's making them happy, get it out of here. Then they could daven.
blocks.title: Reb Zusha and Reb Elimelech in prison

blocks.text: The point of the story is not that the guard took it out. The main thing is that the goal is not to serve G-d only in a certain way, by davening or by going to a *minyan*, which in that situation is not possible. The main point is to serve G-d in whatever situation you are in. The service may look different, but if you appreciate the essence of connecting to G-d, you can find it in any situation.

In a way it does, but it is also something deeper. We are a G-dly spark, and like the soul, which is essentially a living thing and gives life to whatever it comes in contact with, so that it can make a dead body live, an active G-dly spark imbues whatever it touches with G-dliness. That is naturally what a G-dly soul does. If we develop the understanding and awareness to be conscious of that part of ourselves, we can do this *avodah* actively: *bechol drachecha deihu*. That is very connected to bringing *Moshiach*, and it is developing this kind of maturity.
blocks.question: So that presupposes that G-d custom-designs each of our experiences to help us deepen our relationship with Him?

blocks.text: This is what *havein behachma* aims at: both come from getting the depth. When a person has the depth, he can unite *chachma* and *bina*, and gets both the *chachma* of *bina* and the *bina* in *chachma*. Without the depth you have only an external *bina*, and an external *chachma* that sometimes pops in and out, and they do not connect.

In our service we have the animal soul and the G-dly soul, and their service does not relate. The animal soul and the human intellect can understand philosophically that there is a G-d, but that does not inspire it to feel Him or change. The G-dly soul sees G-dliness but cannot find it in the world, so it does not feel connected to the physical world. The two do not relate to each other.

Without the connection between the spiritual and the physical, it goes back and forth: sometimes we feel inspired and G-dly, and sometimes low, not wanting to listen. When the two are connected there is harmony between our human intellect and our G-dly soul, between body and soul, and between G-d and the world. That unity is what this learning and these *yichudim* aim at.

A listener asks whether connecting the two means seeing how a spiritual activity adds value physically and financially. He answers that it is partly that: people care about money, relationships and health, and a spiritual activity like prayer or Torah study can help with them. But it is also that the spiritual is a higher priority than all of these, so it is worth giving them up for it, just as a person gives up money for his health. It is also the source of success in all the other areas, since the G-dly connection feeds ingenuity and creativity.

blocks.text: The fable of the goose that laid golden eggs: its owner got greedy, killed it, thinking its stomach was full of gold, and found only an ordinary stomach inside. That is a *mashal* for this too. The real source of our success and prosperity is our G-dly connection, which is the source of our ingenuity and creativity. To give up the G-dly connection for other things is killing the golden goose.
blocks.title: The golden goose

blocks.text: Just as if you don't take care of your health, it eventually catches up with you and you are not productive, if you don't take care of your soul, nothing else goes well either. It goes many ways, but the point is that it should all be connected, not seen as separate, conflicting things, but as really one thing.
