blocks.text: He goes back over the last point. *Havein behachma* is the ability to explain one idea in many different ways, and it is beyond the grasp of *bina*. It is not about one particular system or explanation, but about seeing how the idea can be expressed in many ways.

sections.title: The navon and the levels of bina: understanding one thing from another
sections.summary: A *navon* is someone who understands one thing from another, a power that comes from the depth of *chachma*. The levels then run from the *chachma* that is beyond any one idea, through *bina sheb'bina* and *chachma sheb'bina*, to the crown of *bina*.

phrases.he: ומה שאמרו נבונים לא אשתכחו,
phrases.en: And this that it says, when Moshe was looking for judges in the desert, he was told to look for certain qualities, and one of them was *nevonim*. But he wasn't able to find *nevonim*.

phrases.he: שהוא המבין דבר מתוך דבר דוקא
phrases.en: A *navon* is someone who can understand one thing from something else.

blocks.text: Moshe, looking for judges in the desert, was told to choose men with certain qualities, and *nevonim* were among them, but he could not find them. A *navon* is someone who understands one thing from another. He asks why this is so hard, and answers from the root of that power, which he takes up next.

phrases.he: היינו מצד שרש כח זה דהבן בחכמה שמגיע בעומק דחכמה הנזכר לעיל,
phrases.en: Because having this power of *havein behachma*, which is what allows you to apply one idea to effectively a different idea, requires that you have the depth of *chachma*. And so it's actually deeper than just the *chachma* itself.

phrases.he: על כן יוכל להבין דבר חכמה אחרת לגמרי מתוך דבר חכמה זאת
phrases.en: And that's why, since he's arriving at the depth of *chachma*, which is beyond any particular *chachma*, he can connect this idea to another idea which is completely externally unrelated.

blocks.text: *Havein behachma* has its root in the depth of *chachma*, so it is deeper than *chachma* itself. From that depth a person can take one *chachma* and understand a completely different one from it, connecting ideas that look unrelated on the surface.

phrases.he: שזהו למעלה במדריגה מן החכם,
phrases.en: And this is higher, this ability is higher than a *chacham*.

phrases.he: דהיינו מגופה של המצאות החכמה זו מאין,
phrases.en: Which is just the idea of being able to conceive of an idea or invent some new idea where he doesn't know where it came from, and he gets this spark of inspiration, he gets this new idea and he understands it.

phrases.he: שאינו מבין ממנה חכמה ושכל אחר
phrases.en: But he won't be able to understand a new *chachma* or a new *sechel* from this idea.

blocks.text: This is higher than a *chacham*: a person gets a flash of a new idea, as if from nothing, and understands it. But he cannot draw any further *chachma* or *sechel* from it. The flash stays limited to that one thing.

The Arizal teaches that one who learns to make *yichudim* can understand one thing from another. Take something you understand, delve into its depth, trace it up to its root, and see how it connects to something else. Then you are never stuck.

*Yichud* means seeing the trail of connections between things, from their concrete form up to their general form, and then back down to some other concrete thing. Two things that seem unrelated on the surface are joined at their root: that is making a *yichud*.
blocks.question: What is the denotation of the term *yichudim*?
Is this pattern recognition?
blocks.text: Making and finding patterns is what *bina* does. When you stare at regular tiles and your mind keeps grouping them, that is your *bina* looking for patterns. *Chachma* is finding something a little beyond the data, its generalization. It can inform pattern recognition, but it is not just that.
The patterns and relationships exist only from a reference point, which is the *chachma* itself: its axioms and perspective. Look at the same thing another way and you will find different patterns.

blocks.title: The vase that is something else
blocks.text: The familiar picture that looks like a vase to most people can also be seen as something else. A person coming to a classroom exercise assumes that what the teacher shows is meaningful, not a joke. Generalize that local assumption and you see how assumptions shape what one sees: the senses do not hand over the information, and the brain does much of the interpreting.

*Chachma* is not an algorithm. A machine can be trained to recognize patterns, but *chachma* is a choice of how to look at something and what to prioritize, and at that level there is no right or wrong answer. Only once a system is set up on a certain *chachma* can it work within that system.

Euclidean and non-Euclidean geometry differ in *chachma*: they start from different axioms about whether space is flat or curved, and each system is self-consistent. Some results, such as whether a triangle has 180 degrees, depend on how one defines space. Relativity is another example: what is moving, and which thing came first, depends on the perspective.

Real depth means you can switch reference points freely, because there is no single true reference point. We are biased to think there is a correct assumption to be found, and that premise is not really true. To appreciate the depth of *chachma* is to see that the approach you take is a choice.

A listener restates the geometry point. The analysis is the same work, comparing parts with the same basic operations, but once the assumptions change those comparisons no longer have to come out equal or unequal, and other possibilities open up.
A listener cites a video about Einstein challenging premises that had been taken as true. Starting from a different premise, one reaches other conclusions, which may be more correct.
With a real appreciation of the depth, you see that any theory or model is only an effective theory: it models one regime or layer of reality well, but never captures all of it.

blocks.title: The biologist and the psychologist
blocks.text: A college professor of his made this point: a biologist and a psychologist each see a different layer of the self. The biologist can treat an acute illness but may not help someone out of a rut or with motivation; the psychologist can work on that layer, but not on the medical side.

blocks.title: The human body
blocks.text: Look at a human body and analyze it. The level of *chachma* is seeing that there is life there, a soul, consciousness, which is not directly in the data you see. The physical things represent a higher, spiritual thing.

phrases.he: (ומכל מקום מה שבהשגה דבינה מבין השגה חדשה מתוך ההשגה זו,
phrases.en: Nevertheless, in a certain way, being able to come up with a new understanding within what you're learning, so learning to analyze something and by having careful analysis you're able to understand it in new ways, even though you're only understanding the concrete, specific example, that is actually, you're connecting to the depth in order to do that.

phrases.he: שרשה בהבן דחכמה,
phrases.en: And so its source is also in this idea of *havanas chachma*, of being able to see the depth of the *chachma*.

phrases.he: שמבין דבר מתוך דבר, רק שזה בהעלם מקור השכל כו' ודי למבין).
phrases.en: That's the idea that we're trying to explain: that if you just focus on the *bina*, even though you're focusing on something that's lower, it's going to also connect up to the source of *chachma*.

blocks.text: Within *bina* too, a person gains a new understanding from the one he already has. Its root is in *havanas chachma*: he understands one thing from another, though the source of the understanding stays hidden. Even when he works on a concrete example he is connecting to the depth, so focusing on *bina* connects up to the source of *chachma*.

phrases.he: ונמצא סדר המדרגות כך הם,
phrases.en: So it comes out that this is the order of things.

phrases.he: בחינת עיון הנזכר לעיל לעמוד על בוריו
phrases.en: So the first thing is this process of *iyun*, of analysis, studying something in depth, which is to dwell on an idea and work on it until you get it very clear.

phrases.he: כו' נקרא בינה שבבינה,
phrases.en: You just clarify all the parts, you can really outline it very clearly and summarize it very succinctly, and that's *bina sheb'bina*.

phrases.he: להבחין תכלית ההבחנה בפנימיות וחיצוניות
phrases.en: to draw very clear distinctions on both its inner aspects and its outer aspects, and to be able to separate the two, what is essential and what circumstantial. Very important part of that analysis process.

blocks.text: The order of the levels is this. The first is *iyun*, dwelling on an idea until every part is clear, so that it can be outlined and summed up briefly: that is *bina sheb'bina*. Within it one draws clear distinctions between the inner and outer aspects of an idea, and between what is essential and what is circumstantial. He calls this a very important part of the analysis.

phrases.he: וגם מזה יוכל להיות בחינת האורך, להוריד ההשגה בלבושים רבים עד שתתגשם להשגות התינוק כנזכר לעיל,
phrases.en: And this process will also give a person the length that they'll be able to explain the idea in very tangibly to the point that a little kid could understand it.

phrases.he: אבל לא בחינת הרוחב בהסברים שונים לכל צד כו'
phrases.en: but they will not have the width, which is the idea of being able to explain, show how you have this idea in many different areas, from many different examples of it.

blocks.text: This process also gives *orech*, length: the idea is brought down in many garments until it is concrete enough for a little child. It does not give *rochav*, the width, which is explaining the idea in different ways from every side.

phrases.he: ואחר כך מבחינת חכמה שבבינה, להמציא חדשות בהשגה א' כנזכר לעיל, הוא הנקרא רוחב,
phrases.en: Then from *chachma* of *bina*, where a person can appreciate new perspectives within this idea, that gives a person a breadth, a width.

phrases.he: וממנו כח דבינה שבבינה העושה בחינת אורך
phrases.en: And actually the hidden source of your ability to explain it simply to a little kid is really a way of practicing it, essentially tapping into this *chachma* of *bina*, because anytime you're taking an idea and you have to bring it out of its natural place, that also requires you tap into the depth to a certain degree.

blocks.text: *Rochav*, the breadth, comes from *chachma sheb'bina*: inventing new perspectives within one grasp. Take Rashi's explanation of a Gemara next to Tosafos's. When you have the depth to appreciate the difference between them, you start to get the breadth of understanding one idea from several perspectives. The *bina sheb'bina* that makes length comes from the same place, and explaining something simply to a little child is a way of practicing that depth.

phrases.he: אבל שיעור האורך והרוחב דחכמה ובינה שבבינה, הוא תלוי בבחינת עומק המושג
phrases.en: but how much the length, how well you can explain it, how simply you can explain it to a little kid, and the width, how much you can see this idea and explain it from different perspectives, different angles, those both depend on the depth.

phrases.he: שנקרא כתר דבינה,
phrases.en: which is the *keser* of *bina*.

phrases.he: וכנראה בחוש שלפי ערך העומק כך יהיה ערך הרוחב והאורך בכל השגת דבר מה וד"ל).
phrases.en: And we see this tangibly, that the deeper a person's understanding, that's exactly proportional to that depth of understanding is going to be how much broad a person's understanding is, and how well they can bring it down.

blocks.text: How much length and width there is, in *chachma* and in *bina sheb'bina*, depends on the depth of the concept, which is the *keser* of *bina*. We see it tangibly: the deeper the understanding, the more simply it can be brought down, and the more ways it can be seen from different perspectives.

sections.title: Daas: the bond that brings depth, length and width
sections.summary: *Daas* is the personal bond with an idea, the feeling that it is one's own. It is not the depth of the concept, but it brings the depth, length and width to the idea, the way *bina* does, and it is the tool that lets a person reach the depth of *chachma*.

phrases.he: ולפ"ז מה שקוראים העולם העמקת הדעת,
phrases.en: So, based on this, it comes out that *amkus hadaas* is not the actual process of studying the idea to get to the depth of the understanding of the idea, which is the depth of *bina*.

phrases.he: אין זה גופה של העמקה, כמו עומק המושג דבינה, שלזה לא יש שייכות לדעת
phrases.en: that doesn't really have a connection to *daas*.

blocks.text: Now *daas*. What the world calls *amkus hadaas*, depth of knowledge, is not the depth of a concept itself. The depth of the concept in *bina* is reached by study, and *daas* has no part in that.

phrases.he: אך הדעת הוא בחינת התקשרות הרגשתו במושג ביותר,
phrases.en: *Daas* is the idea that you're able to experience this idea personally.

phrases.he: והוא שמביא לידי בחינת העמקה במושג, אחר בחינת העיון הנזכר לעיל, שהוא רק כמו בחינת כלי לעומק ההשגה כנזכר לעיל.
phrases.en: And so like we said, the *iyun*, the process of study, is only a tool to arrive at the depth of *bina*, but now we're trying to go further, and so we need this tool of *amkus hadaas* to get further.

blocks.text: *Daas* is being able to experience an idea personally. You can understand something in theory, clearly and well, and it still stays theoretical and detached from reality. *Daas* asks how I can connect this personally, and what its relevance in my life is.

Once a person sees that personal relevance, it carries his understanding to the depth of *chachma*, where he can generalize. The steps are: learn the basic words, outline the idea with all its points until they are clear and how they relate, which is the depth of *bina*. Then find how it applies to your life, and it relates to all of life, not only to one question on Rashi.

This *daas* connection takes a person past analysis. Someone can analyze an idea and explain it well, and it is still cold human intellect. When he senses that the idea is alive for him and could change his life, that motivates him to look deeper into *chachma*. The *iyun* is only a tool for the depth of *bina*; to go further one needs the tool of *amkus hadaas*.

phrases.he: וגם בדעת יש אורך ורוחב ועומק,
phrases.en: So there's also a length, a width, and a depth of that.

phrases.he: כמו יש מי שדעתו קצרה ויש שדעתו ארוכה ויש שדעתו רחבה
phrases.en: some people have a short attention span, some have a long one, and some have a very broad attention; in other words, they are interested in a lot of things, or they can tolerate a lot of opposites.

phrases.he: ולא ארוכה
phrases.en: but it's not so long, so they're not going to really focus on one thing for a long time.

phrases.he: ודעת חזק או דעת קל
phrases.en: and you can have a *daas*, a connection to an idea, to a belief, or whatever you're doing, it could be very strong and something you won't be easily dissuaded from, or it could be something very light, and it's easy to dissuade a person.

phrases.he: כנשים שדעתן קלות,
phrases.en: this is like the idea that it says that women have their daas is light.

phrases.he: הוא בלתי עומק הדעת וממילא דעתו קצרה כו'
phrases.en: because without the depth of *daas*, automatically their connection to things is also shorter.

blocks.text: *Daas*, too, has length, width and depth, as *bina* does. The depth of connection to an idea is reached through its length and width.

*Daas* can be short, long or broad. A broad *daas* is interested in many things and tolerates many opposites, but it does not stay with one thing for long. A *daas* can be strong, so that one is not easily dissuaded from a belief or practice, or light, so that it is easily turned to the opposite.

The line's light *daas*, like women's, he explains: without the depth of *daas* a person's connection to things is shorter, and women, he says, do not tend to become as absorbed in something for long.

sensitivity.reason: A generalisation about women beyond the line: that their connection is shorter and that they do not stay absorbed for long. The line's own words (light daas, like women) are not flagged.
sensitivity.publishable: The line's light *daas*, like women's, he explains: without the depth of *daas* a person's connection to things is shorter.
sensitivity.judgmentNote: Whether his gloss on women's connection prints as said. Precedent: walters-original NOTES records that chapter 1, class 17 (women's daas) was kept as said by the reviewer.

blocks.text: He gives the halacha of *bedikas chametz*: the man is supposed to do the search, because it takes the patience to go over every last thing, which requires much *daas*. Light *daas* is quick to feel, he adds, and women are quick to feel and respond emotionally, much quicker than men.

sensitivity.reason: Generalisations about men and women (who searches for chametz, who feels quickly and emotionally), with the halacha of bedikas chametz framed by them. The halachic point is his explanation of the practice.
sensitivity.publishable: He gives the halacha of *bedikas chametz*: the search takes the patience to go over every last thing, which requires much *daas*. Light *daas* is quick to feel, he adds.
sensitivity.judgmentNote: A person decides whether the gender claims and the halacha of bedikas chametz print as said.

blocks.text: Men have a strong *daas* because they have the two *kavim*, *chesed* and *gevura*, and women have only one, he says, as it is explained elsewhere. A father is more likely to see the value of toughness and discipline. A mother educating her children is, he says, in a masculine role. The same person can be in the position of receiving or giving, depending on the role.

sensitivity.reason: Generalisations about men and women and their roles, beyond the line. The two kavim and the giving and receiving roles are the teaching; the claim about women having one kav is his generalisation.
sensitivity.publishable: Men have a strong *daas* because they have the two *kavim*, *chesed* and *gevura*, as it is explained elsewhere. The same person can be in the position of receiving or giving, depending on the role.
sensitivity.judgmentNote: A person decides whether the gender roles and the claim about one kav print as said, or whether only the two kavim and the roles stay.

phrases.he: והפרש זה בין קלי הדעת לעומקי הדעת, בין גדול לקטן
phrases.en: the difference between having a light connection to something and having a deep connection to something, between big and small, and this is also the difference between maturity and being immature.

phrases.he: ידוע, שהתינוק שדעתו קל, היינו שאין בו כח המרגיש והתקשרות כלל לדבר זה שמבין או רוצה בו, רק בחיצוניות מאד
phrases.en: a child, because he has a light *daas*, that means his feeling of connection to what he wants or understands is not very deep, it's only external. So he wants this external form of the thing, but it's very easy to get him to switch it for something else.

blocks.text: The difference between a light *daas* and a deep *daas* is the difference between big and small, and between maturity and immaturity. A child's *daas* is light: he has no real feeling of connection to what he understands or wants, only to its outside, so he is easily switched to something else.

phrases.he: על כן יתפתה להיפוכו,
phrases.en: and therefore they could be easily, you know, kind of convinced to the opposite.

phrases.he: מה שאין כן הגדול שדעתו עמוקה באותו דבר שמבין או רוצה בו,
phrases.en: but a person who feels a much deeper connection, and connects to the thing on a more abstract level, so they're not as easily shaken by changes of circumstances, or by contradictory arguments and all that kind of stuff.

phrases.he: הוא הנקרא העמקת הדעת,
phrases.en: That's called having a deep *daas*, is when a person connects to this thing in a very deep way, and they feel it's very important to them, and that deep connection is expressed in the fact that they'll tolerate opposites.

phrases.he: שממילא נמשך אורך הדעת ורוחב הדעת כנזכר לעיל בבינה.
phrases.en: That's an example of having that depth being expressed in the width, that they'll be able to weather the storm of all different types of circumstances.

blocks.text: A person whose *daas* is light can be drawn to the opposite. One whose *daas* is deep in what he understands or wants has what is called *amkus hadaas*, and from it the length and width of *daas* follow, as they do in *bina*.

Deep *daas* shows in width. Someone deeply connected tolerates opposites, puts in the hard work and not only when it is easy, and so weathers changing circumstances and the ups and downs. That is the broader *daas*.

Long *daas* means connecting an idea to many words and ways. A passionate person is always talking about it and finding ways to connect to it. To deepen *daas*, work on its length and width: say often the words that express love of G-d and attachment to Him, as in the day's *Tanya* reading.

The Rebbe, often at the start of a *farbrengen*, would find a connection to the day of the week, the day of the month and a person's name. That is the length of *daas*: finding many ways to express it.

blocks.title: The sports fan's hat and jersey
blocks.text: Like a sports fan who wears the hat and the jersey: having all these tangible expressions of connection is the length of *daas*.

blocks.title: A larger book
blocks.text: A student struggling to concentrate was advised to get a larger *sefer*, which fills more of his field of vision. That is also connected to this idea.

blocks.question: Is that related to the verse *uvlechtecha vaderech*, about reviewing your Torah as you go on the way?
blocks.text: Partly. Doing it often is the length, and doing it in many settings, at home, at work and so on, is the width. Connect to something in many diverse places and you get a deep connection to it.

Diversity matters in the channels too, not only in place: words, looking, holding an object, engaging the senses. The mind then perceives a common denominator: this is part of me, however I take information in and wherever I am.

He uses this himself. To learn something quickly and well, he uses these tactics to program his subconscious to get hyper-focused on it: connecting to it often in short stretches, stealing free minutes, toward the end of the night and first thing in the morning.

Connecting in a deep way, in many circumstances, sends the message that something is important, and so one grows more interested in it. The Rebbe's strategies: a mezuzah on every door, which one touches as a reminder, and a *tzedaka* box in every room and in one's business. The aim is for the connection to holiness to touch every part of life, since a connection that holds at home but not outside is not deep.

This keeps a person from feeling meek and afraid of the world, and of opposition. Someone who connects in all these diverse ways gets the fortitude not to feel that it works only if everything is exactly right.

The Rebbe taught that more senses make learning deeper and more lasting: hear it, underline it, write in the margins. A teacher of his advised swaying and walking around while memorizing, to involve the whole body.

He believes the beginning of chapter 3 of *Tanya* makes this point: knowing what is in the books, which is *chachma* and *bina*, does not affect a person's life unless he has the *daas* of constantly connecting to it and thinking about it.

That is the point: find the relevance and make yourself passionate about the idea, so that it is constantly part of your life. *Daas* also means memory and awareness, holding the idea in mind. Without that, even deep *chachma* does not affect a person's *middos* and actions.

A teacher of his taught him the three terms: *chachma*, *bina* and *daas*. *Bina* asks how do I know it is true, and *daas* asks what does it have to do with me. The three, he says, are perception, conceptualization and internalization.

blocks.text: The introduction of the book he names as *Ner Mitzvah v'Torah Ohr* is one he says is worth learning. It begins with a metaphor: a child looking for his father, who is playing hide-and-seek. A foolish child gives up and cries; a wise child follows his father's ways. The challenge to faith in the first *Beis HaMikdash* was spiritual, false prophets and idolatry; from the second *Beis HaMikdash* until now it is lower and physical, and the main challenge is believing false things about other people. The main expression of belief in G-d's unity is seeing the unity between us and our fellow Jew. The ways of G-d that *Chazal* name are the acts of kindness: clothing the naked, hospitality, visiting the sick.

sections.title: Amkus hadaas: focus that narrows, and daas as the root of Moshe's bina
sections.summary: Deep *daas* appears as an intense focus on one idea. *Bina* is the opposite, spreading into breadth, and each needs the other: Moshe, who was *daas*, merited *bina*, the *shaar hanun*.

phrases.he: וסימן להעמקת הדעת
phrases.en: So the sign of *amkus hadaas* is extreme focus, to the point where a person is in the moment totally focused on what he's doing, not hearing anything else or doing anything else, extreme focus of attention.

phrases.he: הוא אשר נראה כענין צמצום וכיווץ כלי המוח, לעוצם עומק התקשרותו במושכל, (בל"א ער איז דרינן פר נומען פר קוועצט שטארק זייער ביז עס3 איז זייער מצומצם רק בתנוע' אחת4 וסקירה אחת לבד כו') שמזה דוקא בא עצם עומק השגה על ידי העיון דבינה
phrases.en: And the other thing of that is just in general obsession, that they're always thinking about this and talking about that.

blocks.text: The depth of *daas* brings the length and width of *daas*, as with *bina*. The sign of deepening *daas* is extreme focus, where a person is wholly absorbed and does not hear anything else, and general obsession: always thinking about the thing and talking about it. Those signs show he finds it very personally relevant and important.

Focus itself is not the point. Training yourself to meditate and empty your mind is a relaxation technique, which the Rebbe recommends as a medical practice for somebody under stress. It should not be confused with religious practice, and it has nothing to do with gaining enlightenment, understanding or *hisbonenus*. Someone who needs it medically is probably not healthy enough for *hisbonenus* of this kind, which could be harmful to him unless he is healthy and stable.

blocks.text: Here the focus is on *hisbonenus* and understanding, and its depth comes from a sense of connection, relevance and empathy to the idea. When the analysis of *bina* is coupled with this *daas*, which feels the idea as deeply relevant and so draws the person in, that is where the real depth of understanding comes: the essence of the idea, not only its external form.

phrases.he: שהוא היפך הצמצום והכיווץ,
phrases.en: now this *bina*, the real understanding, is the opposite of focusing on just one thing, like we said.

phrases.he: שהרי העיון דבינה, גם שעומד ומעוכב בצמצום וכיווץ בתחלתו,
phrases.en: even though with each detail you might be very focused, but you can't get hung up on just one point.

phrases.he: אבל מיד מתפשת לרוחב הרבה בכל פרטי חלקיו, בהבחנת פרטיות הרבה כידוע
phrases.en: the goal of *bina* is specifically to gain a broad data set to get all the points, and compare them and contrast them and see how they all relate to each other and build that structure. And so it's building a *rochav*; it's not just being hyper focused on one point.

blocks.text: *Bina*, the real understanding, is the opposite of focusing on one thing. Even when each detail is studied with focus, you cannot get hung up on one point. The goal of *bina* is a broad set of data: to get all the points, compare and contrast them, and see how they relate and build the structure. That is building *rochav*, the breadth, not hyper-focus on one point.

phrases.he: מה שאין כן הצמצום והכיווץ דהעמקת הדעת, אדרבה, הוא רק הצמצום, שהוא הקיבוץ והאסיפה מכל כח שכלו להתקשר רק במושכל זה
phrases.en: on the other hand, the *daas* is only that focus: you're focusing your attention and your connection just to this one point or this one idea that you are studying, so that you can really be attached to it, really feel it, really sense it.

blocks.text: The narrowing of deepening *daas* is the opposite: it is only a narrowing, a gathering of all one's power to connect to this one idea, so that one really feels it and has the intensity of that experience.

phrases.he: שזה היפך בחינת התפשטות העיון בהרחבת ענין המושכל,
phrases.en: which is the opposite of the expansion of the idea when you're analyzing. You're trying to pull it apart and break it down to all of its parts, which is an expansion of the ideas, as opposed to a focus to really experience the idea.

phrases.he: (בל"א דער קלעפ מיט דעם אריין לייגין זיך גאר כו')
phrases.en: the focus, and like really being obsessed with something, really being absorbed in something.

phrases.he: ואמנם על ידי העמקת הדעת בא לידי עמקות המושכל עד שרשו בעמקי החכמה ובינה
phrases.en: Nevertheless, it's through this depth of *daas* that a person will get the real depth of the idea, both the depth of *chachma* and the depth of *bina*.

blocks.text: This is the opposite of *iyun*, which spreads out to widen an idea. Without deep *daas*, a person has trouble pulling an idea apart to focus on its details, because the details do not carry the same experience. Deep interest changes that.

blocks.title: Taking the iPhone apart
blocks.text: A consumer wants the finished phone that works out of the box. Someone who wants to build one and reverse-engineer it will want to understand every part and why it works, because his interest is deeper. Deep *daas* gives the patience for the details, even though each detail distracts from the goal of seeing the whole.

The book returns to this in chapter 4: the balance of the *klal* and the *prat*. The goal is the big picture, but the only way to get it is to spend the time on all the details and then put them together.

The Yiddish phrase for this is being absorbed in something, really obsessed with it. Through this depth of *daas* a person gets the real depth of the idea, both the depth of *chachma* and the depth of *bina*.

phrases.he: (עד בחינת דעת עליון דמזווג חכמה לבינה
phrases.en: and then there's this upper *daas*, which is what unites *chachma* and *bina*.

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב למעלה בענין עומק המושג דבינה,
phrases.en: like we explained before, the depth of *bina*, the real essence of that depth, the *shaar hanun*, goes all the way up to the depth of *chachma*.

phrases.he: והיינו דדעת גנוז בפומא דאימא כו'
phrases.en: and this is what it says, that *daas* is hidden in the mouth of *Imma*, in the mouth of *bina*.

blocks.text: There is an upper *daas* that unites *chachma* and *bina*, as explained above under the depth of the concept of *bina*. It comes from the *keser*. When a person gets this deeper connection he can fuse *chachma* and *bina* and move between them. That is *davar mitoch davar*, and the real idea of *yichud* is to go from the physical up to the spiritual and back down to the physical.

The depth of *bina*, its *shaar hanun*, goes all the way up to the depth of *chachma*. A person's interest reaches beyond the application to the general abstraction, because he sees how it helps in other applications here in this world, not only to study philosophy.

blocks.title: Entering the Pardes in peace
blocks.text: I think this is the idea of the four who went into the *Pardes*: Rabbi Akiva came out because he went in in peace and came out in peace. Going in with peace means your intention in the study is to bring it back and apply it to the world, not to lose yourself in spiritual philosophy.
The line says that *daas* is hidden in the mouth of *Imma*, which is *bina*.

phrases.he: וכמו שאמרו, משה שהוא הדעת,
phrases.en: like it says, that Moshe, because he was a person of *daas*, merited *bina*.

phrases.he: זכה לבינה שהוא שער הנון,
phrases.en: and that's the idea that Moshe merited the *shaar hanun*, the essence of the understanding,

phrases.he: כי הא בהא תליא,
phrases.en: because they're interdependent.

phrases.he: וכמה שכתוב בכתבים בכמה דוכתי ודי למבין.
phrases.en: and like it's explained in the *kisvei* many places.

blocks.text: Moshe, who was a person of *daas*, merited *bina*. The two are linked, and true understanding comes through the depth of *daas*.

Moshe merited the *shaar hanun*, the essence of understanding. Only someone learning with deep personal connection and relevance gets the true depth of the Torah, and that ties back to *ahavas Yisrael*.

blocks.title: Moshe breaks the luchos
blocks.text: Moshe broke the *luchos* to save the Jewish people and the *erev rav*. That shows the essence of the Torah is beyond the Torah itself: it is for the sake of the Jewish people. He had *mesirus nefesh* and said, *mecheini na mi'sifrecha*, erase me from Your book.

The last verse of the Torah says Moshe did everything before the eyes of all Israel. Rashi asks what the great thing was, and answers that it was breaking the *luchos*, for which Hashem said, *yasher koach*. So the greatest thing Moshe ever did was smashing the *luchos*.

Moshe was a man of truth, and his whole life was focused on bringing people to truth. At the time of the golden calf he uncovered a deeper truth: the reason he cares about truth is what it does for people, so he was willing to set truth aside to help them. That brought the essence of the Torah we have today, which is higher than the first *luchos*.
Analysis brings a person to understanding, and the sense of personal relevance lets him reach the real depth. The two depend on each other, as is explained in the *Kisvei* in many places.

He thinks that *Kisvei*, the manuscripts, here refers to the later *maamarim* of the Alter Rebbe, the longer ones written after Petersburg, which are similar in style to the Mitteler Rebbe's. Many of the Mitteler Rebbe's *maamarim* are expansions on them.

blocks.question: Does Reb Hillel Paritcher's commentary place the source of *daas* in *keser*, under the name *chushim*, which may mean talents?
blocks.text: He vaguely recalls that it does, if he is not mistaken, and that the commentary labels it *chushim*, which he says here means sensitivity rather than talents. Talent relates to it, since when a person is very tuned into something and has a sensitivity for it, he will be talented in it.

blocks.question: Is this a G-d-given proclivity, a natural interest at the level of *taanug* within *keser*, as with a musical prodigy who is sensitive to music from childhood?
blocks.text: He answers that, in a similar way, every G-dly soul has a natural sense for G-dliness. *Daas* comes from *keser*, which is a person's identity and his delight, and so it comes from the *yechida* of a Jew.

The point of this chapter is that the G-dly connection, which is revealed through *chachma* and faith, is uncovered by learning, but by detailed study grounded in what can be understood in the world. General words of faith, such as "there is only one G-d", not grounded in the particulars, lead to fantasies.

By contrast, when a person understands G-d by seeing the greatness of His handiwork, looking at the details of creation, a flower, a squirrel, and the mundane things around us, and connects that to personal relevance, the depth of understanding opens in physical things, and in his faith and his G-dly soul. That kind of learning is what we are after.
He agrees: the power of *daas* may come from an interest at the level of desire, and that may trace back to the nature of the soul that G-d gave him.
blocks.question: If someone at work is interested in solving a real problem, does the interest start earlier, in the choice of field, and trace back to a natural interest, such as an analytic mind?

blocks.text: A listener points out that this leads to *ahavas olam*, which we say before *Krias Shema*. He agrees: learning in depth from the world itself, to appreciate G-d better, leads there.

The love of the G-dly soul is not connected to the world, but it must be grounded in *hisbonenus* in the world and in *memalei kol almin*, the things we can see and understand in creation. That is what connects the G-dly soul to the animal soul. If a person wakes up the faith of the G-dly soul alone, it does not carry the animal soul along. The two are divided and fight, and he feels connected only in a secluded state, while in the world it drags him down.

He asks whether the listener knows the parable of the princess and the peasant in the *Zohar*. He thinks it is from the *Ramchal*, though it could be based on the *Zohar*. The listener had heard it that way, and neither of them knows the whole *Zohar* well.

blocks.title: The princess and the peasant
blocks.text: A princess and a peasant were in love, and the king exiled them, and they married. The husband did right by her: he brought her food and kept the cabin nice and watertight. But she sometimes grew wistful, remembering the dances and music of the castle. He guessed she wanted carrots, then radishes, but what she yearned for was something he could not provide, and she loved him too much to say what she was missing.
He's a peasant, he thinks like a peasant.

sensitivity.reason: Characterises peasants as a group that thinks in a limited way. It is a remark about a social group, not part of the parable.
sensitivity.publishable: He is a simple man who thinks in his own terms.

blocks.text: The husband wants to please her, but he does not know that what she yearns for is outside his framework. She loves him very much, but she cannot bring herself to say what she is missing.
That is the *mashal* of the body and the soul. With *Chassidus* we try to bring the two together; he jokes that this is a kind of marriage counseling.

He returns to the pattern recognition he mentioned earlier. Each world in the *seder hishtalshelus* is a *mashal* for the next: they share the ten *sefiros* and a certain interaction, but they are at entirely different levels.

blocks.title: Waves
blocks.text: Light waves, sound waves, seismic waves and waves in water have different mediums, but there is a commonality of the wave itself, like the pattern recognition of *bina*. He once said this to someone.
